newsitem.title: UK: Bosnia conference takes stock of year-old peace.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia conference takes stock of year-old peace.

text.p: Ministers from more than 50 countries meet in London this week to take stock of the year-old Bosnian peace process and discuss how to tackle major problems that international efforts have so far failed to resolve.

A year after the Bosnian rivals hammered out a peace deal in Dayton, Ohio to end the 43-month war, the divided country shows few signs of sticking to the civilian elements of the agreement designed to help bury old hatreds.
"It is time we again pressed the main players in the Balkan drama to live up to their commitments," said a European diplomat who asked to remain anonymous.

Foreign ministers from Europe and North America, Russia, Bosnia, Croatia and Yugoslavia, as well as officials from the major aid agencies, will discuss the problems during a two-day Peace Implementation Conference on Wednesday and Thursday.
They will focus on the issues of war criminals, the return of refugees, freedom of movement, continuing divisions in the town of Mostar and rebuilding Bosnia's wrecked economy.
The guns in Bosnia are silent today and armies confined to their barracks, thanks mainly to the 50,000 well-armed members of the NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR).
But sceptics say Dayton is merely a very expensive ceasefire rather than a permanent solution to a conflict that killed some 200,000 people and displaced two million others.

NATO has already agreed to keep a 30,000-strong follow-on force in Bosnia for the next 18 months while the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has extended its mandate to monitor local elections planned for next year.

The follow-on force still looks to be a crucial element to the peace process, especially as military sources at the OSCE say neither the Moslem-Croat Federation nor the Bosnian Serbs are meeting arms control commitments agreed a year ago.

Dayton also said war criminals were supposed to face justice before the Hague war crimes tribunal but many are still at large, notably former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic.
There should have been porous administrative boundaries between the republic and the federation but nationalists have turned them into borders and crossing them can be lethal.
And within the federation itself, the Moslems and Croats are often at each others' throats.
The southern town of Mostar, meant to be the symbol of their new-found unity, is still almost as divided as it was during a vicious 10-month local the two sides fought in 1993.
Diplomats say the process of restoring mutual confidence after such destruction and hatred is a slow and painful process.
"That is why we are preparing for the process. IFOR is staying, OSCE is staying, the $1.8 billion in reconstruction carrot is there.
"So is the stick -- oblivion if the parties chose recalcitrance instead of reason," said one Western diplomat.
As if this were not enugh, the planned Bosnian joint institutions have been painfully slow to get off the ground.
The three-man presidency was formed only after a one-month delay but there is no sign of a government being put together.

In another sign of the potential for conflict, the driving forces behind the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia -- presidents Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Franjo Tudjman of Croatia -- will not attend the London meeting.
Both strongmen, hard-pressed at home by popular protests against their rule, are sending their foreign ministers instead.
